claim: Drosophila neuroblasts are temporally patterned by sequentially expressed Temporal Transcription Factors (TTFs).
source: Drosophila neuroblasts are temporally patterned by sequentially expressed Temporal Transcription Factors (TTFs).
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field, referenced in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Direct transcriptional regulation between TTFs has not been verified in most cases.
source: These TTFs are proposed to form a transcriptional cascade based on mutant phenotypes, although direct transcriptional regulation between TTFs has not been verified in most cases.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The expression of TTFs Sloppy-paired 1/2 (Slp1/2) is directly regulated at the transcriptional level by two other TTFs and the cell-cycle dependent Notch signaling through two cis-regulatory elements.
source: We use neuroblasts of the Drosophila optic lobe medulla to address these questions and show that the expression of TTFs Sloppy-paired 1/2 (Slp1/2) is directly regulated at the transcriptional level by two other TTFs and the cell-cycle dependent Notch signaling through two cis-regulatory elements.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including enhancer identification, mutagenesis, and reporter assays.

claim: Supplying constitutively active Notch can rescue the delayed transition into the Slp stage in cell cycle arrested neuroblasts.
source: We also show that supplying constitutively active Notch can rescue the delayed transition into the Slp stage in cell cycle arrested neuroblasts.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript with data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Neuroblasts in the embryonic ventral nerve cord (VNC) are temporally patterned by a TTF cascade Hunchback (Hb), Kruppel (Kr), Nubbin/Pdm2 (Pdm), Castor (Cas), and Grainy head (Grh).
source: For example, neuroblasts in the embryonic ventral nerve cord (VNC) are temporally patterned by a TTF cascade Hunchback (Hb), Kruppel (Kr), Nubbin/Pdm2 (Pdm), Castor (Cas), and Grainy head (Grh) (Brody and Odenwald, 2000; Isshiki et al., 2001; Grosskortenhaus et al., 2006; Baumgardt et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila optic lobe medulla neuroblasts utilize a TTF cascade composed of Homothorax (Hth), SoxNeuro (SoxN), Doublesex-Mab related 99B (Dmrt99B), Odd paired (Opa), Eyeless (Ey), Earmuff (Erm), Homeobrain (Hbn), Sloppy-paired (Slp1,Slp2), Scarecrow (Scro), Dichaete (D), BarH1/2, Tailless (Tll), and Glial cell missing (Gcm).
source: while Drosophila optic lobe medulla neuroblasts utilize a different TTF cascade composed of Homothorax (Hth), SoxNeuro (SoxN), Doublesex-Mab related 99B (Dmrt99B), Odd paired (Opa), Eyeless (Ey), Earmuff (Erm), Homeobrain (Hbn), Sloppy-paired (Slp1,Slp2), Scarecrow (Scro), Dichaete (D), BarH1/2, Tailless (Tll), and Glial cell missing (Gcm) ( Suzuki et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2022; Konstantinides et al., 2022; Li et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In the embryonic TTF cascade, cytokinesis is required for the first transition (Hb to Kr) but all later temporal transitions progress normally in G2-arrested neuroblasts.
source: In the embryonic VNC TTF cascade, cytokinesis is required for the first transition (Hb to Kr) and acts by promoting the nuclear export of seven-up (svp) mRNA encoding a switching factor, but all later temporal transitions progress normally in G2-arrested neuroblasts (Isshiki et al., 2001; Grosskortenhaus et al., 2005; Mettler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In larval VNC NBs, timely transition from the Imp/Castor/Chinmo to Syncrip/Broad stage requires cell cycle progression.
source: In larval VNC NBs, timely transition from the Imp /Castor/Chinmo to Syncrip/Broad stage also requires cell cycle progression (van den Ameele and Brand, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: During the asymmetric division of Drosophila neuroblasts, Numb is asymmetrically localized to the intermediate progenitor, resulting in unidirectional Delta-Notch signaling from the intermediate progenitor to the neuroblast.
source: During the asymmetric division of Drosophila neuroblasts, Numb, a negative regulator of Notch signaling, is asymmetrically localized to the intermediate progenitor, resulting in unidirectional Delta-Notch signaling from the intermediate progenitor to the neuroblast (Knoblich et al., 1995; Rhyu et al., 1994; Roegiers and Jan, 2004; Fuerstenberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Slp1 and Slp2 are two homologous fork-head family transcription factors expressed in the same temporal pattern in medulla neuroblasts.
source: Among the TTFs, Slp1 and Slp2 are two homologous fork-head family transcription factors expressed in the same temporal pattern in medulla neuroblasts (Figure 1B–B''').
evidence: This is demonstrated by the expression patterns shown in Figure 1B-B'''.

claim: Slp expression is activated by Ey and Slp in turn represses Ey expression.
source: Slp was the first medulla TTF whose regulatory relationship with the previous TTF Ey was clearly understood from genetic studies: Slp expression is activated by Ey and Slp in turn represses Ey expression (Suzuki et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The expression patterns of slp1 and slp2 mRNA closely parallel the expression of Slp1 and Slp2 proteins.
source: The observed patterns of slp1 and slp2 mRNA expression closely parallel the expression of Slp1 and Slp2 proteins (Figure 1B–D'''')
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing mRNA and protein expression patterns in Figure 1.

claim: The expression of slp1 and slp2 is directly regulated at transcription.
source: The observed patterns of slp1 and slp2 mRNA expression closely parallel the expression of Slp1 and Slp2 proteins (Figure 1B–D''''), and are also corroborated by scRNA-seq data (Zhu et al., 2022), indicating that the expression of slp1 and slp2 is directly regulated at transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel expression of mRNA and protein, and supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: A 220 bp enhancer element activates GFP expression in medulla neuroblasts in the same pattern as endogenous Slp1 and Slp2.
source: A 220 bp enhancer element located within the REDfly enhancer u8772 activates GFP expression in medulla neuroblasts in the same pattern as endogenous Slp1 and Slp2 in reporter assays.
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 2B-B'''.

claim: An 850 bp enhancer segment drives reporter expression that closely coincides with the expressions of endogenous Slp1 and Slp2, although it is initiated at a slightly later temporal stage than the 220 bp enhancer.
source: Reporter GFP expression driven by an 850 bp enhancer segment located within the REDfly enhancer d5778 also closely coincides with the expressions of endogenous Slp1 and Slp2, although it is initiated at a slightly later temporal stage than the 220 bp enhancer.
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 2C-C'''.

claim: Deletion of both the 220 bp and 850 bp enhancers results in loss of Slp1 and Slp2 expression in medulla neuroblasts.
source: A CRISPR-Cas9 edited chromosome 2 with both enhancers deleted (indicated as SlpDED) when placed over the SlpS37A chromosome results in loss of Slp1 and Slp2 expression in medulla neuroblasts in affected flies (n=11).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CRISPR deletion experiments shown in Figure 2D-D''''.

claim: The u8772 220 bp and d5778 850 bp enhancers act together and are necessary and specific enhancers for Slp1 and Slp2 expressions in medulla neuroblasts and progeny.
source: This result confirms that these two enhancers acting together are necessary and specific enhancers for Slp1 and Slp2 expressions in medulla neuroblasts and progeny.
evidence: This is concluded from the double enhancer deletion experiment.

claim: Potential binding sites for Ey, Su(H), Slp1, and Scro/Vnd were identified in the slp enhancers.
source: This initial analysis predicted the occurrence of putative binding sites for the previous TTF Ey, the CSL transcription factor Su(H), Slp1 itself, and an Nk2-class homeodomain transcription factor Ventral nervous system defective (Vnd) (Figure 3, Table 2, Supplementary file 3) in our enhancers.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis using FIMO and other tools.

claim: Slp2 expression is delayed in N-RNAi clones compared to wild-type neuroblasts.
source: In control regions, Slp2 is turned on at the 4th- 5th neuroblast from the lateral edge, while in N-RNAi clones (n=12), Slp2 is turned on at the 10th-15th neuroblast.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4A-A'''.

claim: Slp2 expression is delayed in Su(H)-RNAi clones.
source: Similarly, Slp2 expression initiates between the 7th and 10th neuroblasts inside Su(H)-RNAi clones (n=11).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4B-B'''.

claim: Slp2 expression is delayed in clones expressing dominant-negative Mastermind.
source: Within mamDN expressing clones (n=6), Slp2 is initiated between the 7th and 10th neuroblast as with Su(H) RNAi clones.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 4C-C'''.

claim: Timing of Slp1/2 expression in medulla neuroblasts is regulated by the Notch pathway.
source: These data suggest that timing of Slp1/2 expression in medulla neuroblasts is regulated by the Notch pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown experiments of Notch pathway components.

claim: Delta is expressed in medulla neuroblasts and their progeny GMCs.
source: Of these only UAS-GFP driven by delta-Gal4 was seen to be expressed in medulla neuroblasts and in their progeny GMCs.
evidence: This is based on expression analysis of Notch ligands.

claim: Knockdown of Delta causes a delay in Slp2 expression.
source: In neuroblasts within Dl-RNAi expression clones, Slp2 expression is initiated at the 6th-10th neuroblasts from the medulla lateral edge (Figure 4D–D''') (n=5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4D-D'''.

claim: Notch signaling is required for the timely transition into the Ey stage.
source: Ey is normally turned on in the 2nd-3rd neuroblast. In N-RNAi clones, Ey is turned on in the 5th-8th neuroblast (n=6) (Figure 5A1-A8), suggesting that Notch signaling is required for the timely transition into the Ey stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining Ey expression in N-RNAi clones.

claim: In N-RNAi clones, the transition to the Slp stage occurs in the 6th-9th Ey+ neuroblast.
source: In N-RNAi clones, the transition to the Slp stage occurs in the 6th-9th Ey +neuroblast (n=6) (Figure 5A1-A8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining the Ey to Slp transition in N-RNAi clones.

claim: In Su(H) mutant clones, the transition to the Slp stage occurs after the 6th-8th Ey+ neuroblasts.
source: In Su(H) mutant clones, the transition occurs after the 6th-8th Ey +neuroblasts (n=5)(Figure 5B–C'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining the Ey to Slp transition in Su(H) mutant clones.

claim: Overexpression of Ey in Su(H) mutant clones does not rescue the delayed Slp transition.
source: To make sure the delayed Slp transition is not mediated through Ey with loss of Su(H), we supplied Ey using a dpn-Gal4 and UAS-Ey in Su(H) mutant clones. In such clones, Ey is over-expressed, but the transition to Slp stage is still delayed to the 6th-7th Ey +neuroblast (n=6) (Figure 5D–E'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5D-E''.

claim: Notch signaling facilitates the Ey to Slp transition in addition to an earlier indirect role through Ey.
source: These results suggest that Notch signaling also facilitates the Ey to Slp transition in addition to an earlier indirect role through Ey.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the Slp transition is delayed even when Ey is overexpressed in Su(H) mutant clones.

claim: Supplying active NICD is not sufficient to rescue Slp expression in ey-RNAi clones.
source: Supplying NICD using a dpn >FRT-stop-FRT3-FRT-NICD transgene (which drives the expression of NICD from the dpn enhancer in presence of heat shock activated Flippase; see Materials and methods) was not sufficient to rescue Slp expression in ey-RNAi clones (Figure 5I–I'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5I-I''.

claim: Overexpression of Scro is not sufficient to rescue Slp expression in ey-RNAi clones.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Scro was also not sufficient to rescue Slp expression in ey-RNAi clones (Figure 5J–J'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5J-J''.

claim: The previous TTF Ey is required to initiate Slp expression, while Notch signaling and Scro require Ey to further activate Slp expression and facilitate the timely transition to the Slp stage.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the previous TTF Ey is required to initiate Slp expression, while Notch signaling and Scro require Ey to further activate Slp expression and facilitate the timely transition to the Slp stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of the genetic experiments.

claim: GFP reporter expression driven by both the 220 bp and 850 bp enhancers is lost in ey-RNAi clones.
source: For both enhancers, GFP reporter expression and Slp2 expression were lost in ey-RNAi clones (Figure 6A–B''')
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays in ey-RNAi clones shown in Figure 6A-B'''.

claim: GFP reporter expression driven by both the 220 bp and 850 bp enhancers is lost or delayed in su(H)-RNAi clones.
source: Similarly, GFP reporter expression was lost or delayed in su(H)-RNAi clones for both enhancers (Figure 6C–D''')
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays in su(H)-RNAi clones shown in Figure 6C-D'''.

claim: Reporter expression driven by both the 220 bp and 850 bp enhancers within slp LOF neuroblasts is normal.
source: Reporter expression driven by both enhancers within slp LOF neuroblasts is normal as in wild-type neuroblasts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays in slp LOF clones shown in Figure 6E-F'.

claim: Slp1/2 are not required to initiate their own expression.
source: Though this suggests that Slp1/2 are not required to initiate their own expression, it does not preclude a possible role of Slp1/2 in sustaining their own expression in older Slp1/2 stage neuroblasts or progeny
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reporter expression is normal in slp LOF clones.

claim: Deletion or mutation of Ey binding sites in the 220 bp enhancer nearly eliminates GFP expression.
source: For the u8772 220 bp enhancer, individual deletion of one Ey binding site (220-Ey-Site1) or mutation of another Ey binding site (220-Ey-Site2) nearly eliminated GFP expression (Figure 7B–C''' and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7B-C''' and H.

claim: Mutation of all four predicted Su(H) sites in the 220 bp enhancer leads to a complete loss of GFP expression.
source: Mutation of all four predicted Su(H) sites in the u8772 220 bp enhancer led to a complete loss of GFP expression from the reporter (Figure 7D–D''' and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7D-D''' and H.

claim: Mutation of two Su(H) sites that are perfect matches to the consensus in the 220 bp enhancer causes a dramatic reduction of reporter expression.
source: We also generated another reporter mutating only the two Su(H) sites that were perfect matches to the consensus, and this caused a dramatic reduction of the reporter expression (Figure 7E–E''' and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7E-E''' and H.

claim: Mutation of the Scro/Vnd site in the 220 bp enhancer greatly reduces the level of GFP expression.
source: Mutation of the Scro/Vnd site in the u8772 220 bp enhancer greatly reduced the level of GFP expression (Figure 7F–F''' and H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7F-F''' and H.

claim: Mutation of Slp1 binding sites in the 220 bp enhancer significantly reduces the level of GFP expression but preserves the pattern.
source: Mutation of Slp1 binding sites significantly reduced the level of GFP expression, but preserved the pattern of GFP expression as the wild type GFP reporter (Figure 7G–G''' and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7G-G''' and H.

claim: Combined deletion and mutation of three predicted Ey binding sites in the 850 bp enhancer abolishes reporter expression.
source: For the d5778 850 bp reporter, combined deletion and mutation of three predicted Ey binding sites abolished the reporter expression
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 8B-B''' and E.

claim: Deletion of seven possible Scro binding sites in the 850 bp enhancer reduces reporter expression greatly.
source: while deletion of seven possible Scro binding sites reduced the reporter expression greatly (Figure 8B–C''' and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 8C-C''' and E.

claim: Deletion of the putative Slp1 binding site in the 850 bp enhancer does not significantly change GFP reporter expression.
source: Deletion of the putative Slp1 binding site did not significantly change the GFP reporter expression (Figure 8D–D''').
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 8D-D'''.

claim: Mutation of Su(H) binding sites in the 850 bp enhancer increases GFP expression in neuroblasts.
source: For both variants, GFP expression is greatly intensified in glial cells, making it difficult to assess the neuroblast expression (Figure 9—figure supplement 1). Therefore, we used repoGal4 to knock down GFP expression in glial cells using UAS-GFP-RNAi, and found that the neuroblast GFP expression was actually increased compared to the wild-type reporter for both variants (Figure 9B–C''' and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 9B-C''' and D.

claim: Su(H) does not activate slp1/slp2 expression through the d5778 850 bp enhancer directly.
source: These data suggest that Notch signaling does not activate this enhancer directly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutation of Su(H) sites increases reporter expression.

claim: Notch signaling may activate slp1/2 expression by acting on the u8772 220 bp enhancer alone.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that Notch signaling may activate slp1/2 expression by acting on the u8772 220 bp enhancer alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined mutagenesis results.

claim: Reproducible peaks of Ey and Su(H) binding were observed in the genomic region corresponding to the identified enhancers of Slp1/2 transcription.
source: Reproducible peaks of Ey and Su(H) binding were observed in both replicates in the genomic region corresponding to the identified enhancers of Slp1/2 transcription, although reproducible Su(H) peaks were observed only in a smaller region toward the 3' end of the d5778 enhancer, in contrast to the u8772 220 bp enhancer where Su(H) peaks are distributed prominently throughout the enhancer body (Figure 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DamID-sequencing experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: Peaks of Ey binding were observed in the genomic region of the scro gene.
source: We also observed peaks of Ey binding in the genomic region of scro gene (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the observation that Scro expression is initiated in medulla neuroblasts at about the same time as Slp1/2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DamID-sequencing experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Notch signaling is largely lost in cell-cycle arrested neuroblasts.
source: In the region where PCNA is knocked down, a large fraction of neuroblasts don't express E(spl)mγGFP, a Notch signaling reporter (Campos-Ortega, 1988), while all neuroblasts in the control regions express E(spl)mγGFP (Figure 11A–A'''). Thus, Notch signaling is largely lost in cell-cycle arrested neuroblasts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining Notch reporter expression in PCNA-RNAi neuroblasts shown in Figure 11A-A'''.

claim: In PCNA-RNAi neuroblasts, Ey expression is reduced and Slp2 expression is lost.
source: In affected region marked by loss of PCNA staining, Ey expression is reduced and Slp2 expression is lost in Dpn +neuroblasts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining Ey and Slp2 expression in PCNA-RNAi neuroblasts shown in Figure 11C-C''''.

claim: Cell cycle progression is required for the precise timing of Ey to Slp1/2 transition.
source: Thus, cell cycle progression is also required for the precise timing of Ey to Slp1/2 transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Slp2 expression is delayed when cell cycle is arrested or slowed down.

claim: Supplying NICD is sufficient to rescue Slp2 expression in PCNA-RNAi clones.
source: Supplying NICD was sufficient to rescue Slp2 expression in PCNA-RNAi clones (Figure 11G–H'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 11G-H''.

claim: For the Ey to Slp transition, the presence of active Notch signaling can substitute for the requirement of the cell-cycle progression.
source: This suggests that for the Ey to Slp transition, the presence of active Notch signaling can substitute for the requirement of the cell-cycle progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that supplying NICD rescues Slp2 expression in cell-cycle arrested neuroblasts.

claim: Supplying active NICD in wild type condition does not significantly affect the timing of the Ey to Slp transition.
source: In wild type condition, supplying active NICD did not significantly affect the timing of the Ey to Slp transition, which is still around 3rd-4th Ey +neuroblast (Figure 11I–J''')
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining the Ey to Slp transition in wild type neuroblasts with NICD overexpression shown in Figure 11I-J'''.

claim: The cis-regulatory elements of TTF genes in the embryonic and medulla TTF cascades haven't been characterized in most cases.
source: However, with a few exceptions (Hirono et al., 2012), the cis-regulatory elements of these TTF genes haven't been characterized.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: It is not known whether cross-regulations among TTFs are indeed direct transcriptional regulations.
source: Thus, it is not known whether these cross-regulations are indeed direct transcriptional regulations.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: In the embryonic TTF cascade, loss of one TTF often does not block temporal progression, but only causes the corresponding fates to be skipped.
source: Moreover, in the embryonic TTF cascade, although mis-expression of one TTF is sufficient to activate the next TTF and repress the 'next plus one' TTF, loss of one TTF often does not block temporal progression, but only causes the corresponding fates to be skipped (Isshiki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the medulla TTF cascade, one TTF is required but not sufficient to promote the TTF cascade progression.
source: In the medulla TTF cascade, one TTF is required but not sufficient to promote the TTF cascade progression (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Additional mechanisms besides cross-regulations among TTFs might function to regulate TTF progression.
source: These studies suggest that additional mechanisms besides cross-regulations among TTFs might function to regulate TTF progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that TTFs are not always sufficient to promote progression.

claim: The requirement of cell-cycle progression varies depending on the specific temporal transition.
source: These results suggest that the requirement of cell-cycle progression varies depending on the specific temporal transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the different requirements for cell cycle progression in different temporal transitions.

claim: In the vertebrate cortex, the temporal transition from generating deep layer neurons to generating upper layer neurons is not affected by blocking cell cycle progression when constitutively active Notch signaling is provided.
source: In the vertebrate cortex, the temporal transition from generating deep layer neurons to generating upper layer neurons is not affected by blocking cell cycle progression when constitutively active Notch signaling is provided to maintain the un-differentiated status of cortical neural progenitors (Okamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Upon binding to a ligand from a neighboring cell, the Notch receptor is cleaved to release the Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which then enters the nucleus and associates with the DNA-binding protein CSL.
source: Upon binding to a ligand from a neighboring cell, the Notch receptor is cleaved to release the Notch intracellular domain (NICD), which then enters the nucleus and associates with the DNA-binding protein CSL (CBF1/RBPjκ/Su(H)/Lag-1).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of Notch signaling.

claim: The NICD-CSL complex recruits the transcriptional coactivator Mastermind (MAM) to activate transcription of Notch target genes.
source: The NICD-CSL then recruits the transcriptional coactivator Mastermind (MAM) to activate transcription of Notch target genes, mainly the bHLH transcriptional repressors of the HES (hairy and enhancer of split) /HEY families (reviewed in Fortini, 2009; Kopan and Ilagan, 2009; Bray and Furriols, 2001).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of Notch signaling, supported by citations.

claim: Ectopic activation of Notch signaling in the progeny causes them to revert into neuroblasts and over-proliferate.
source: Ectopic activation of Notch signaling in the progeny causes them to revert into neuroblasts and over-proliferate, while inhibition of Notch signaling in type II NBs eliminates the whole lineage (Wang et al., 2006; Bowman et al., 2008; Weng et al., 2010; Zacharioudaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In most type I NB lineages, loss of N signaling does not affect neuroblast maintenance.
source: In contrast, in most type I NB lineages, loss of N signaling does not affect neuroblast maintenance, and it was shown that E(spl) complex proteins and Deadpan act redundantly to maintain the un-differentiated state (stemness) of neuroblasts by repressing differentiation genes (Zacharioudaki et al., 2012; Almeida and Bray, 2005; Magadi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Notch signaling is involved in controlling the daughter cell proliferation modes specifically the type I to type 0 switch in embryonic VNC NBs.
source: Notch signaling is also involved in controlling the daughter cell proliferation modes specifically the type I to type 0 switch in embryonic VNC NBs (Ulvklo et al., 2012; Bivik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During the asymmetric division of neural progenitors in vertebrates, the more differentiated progeny expresses Delta and activates Notch signaling in the sister cell to maintain the neural progenitor fate.
source: Work in the vertebrate central nervous system suggests that during the asymmetric division of neural progenitors, the more differentiated progeny expresses Delta and activates Notch signaling in the sister cell to maintain the neural progenitor fate (reviewed in Moore and Alexandre, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Notch signaling shows cell-cycle-dependent activation and the expression of the Notch target Hes genes oscillates during the cell cycle in neural progenitors.
source: In addition, Notch signaling shows cell-cycle-dependent activation and the expression of the Notch target Hes genes oscillates during the cell cycle in neural progenitors (reviewed in Kageyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Whether Notch signaling also has a role in temporal transitions between TTFs has not been investigated.
source: Although Notch signaling has been shown to play many important roles in neural lineage development, whether Notch signaling also has a role in temporal transitions between TTFs has not been investigated.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: In the larval optic lobe, a neurogenesis wave spreads in a medial to lateral direction to sequentially convert neuroepithelial cells into medulla neuroblasts.
source: In the larval optic lobe, a neurogenesis wave spreads in a medial to lateral direction to sequentially convert neuroepithelial cells into medulla neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a well-established feature of medulla development.

claim: Medulla neuroblasts of different ages are orderly aligned on the lateral to medial spatial axis with the youngest on the lateral side.
source: As a result, medulla neuroblasts of different ages are orderly aligned on the lateral to medial spatial axis with the youngest on the lateral side (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established feature of medulla development, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Medulla neuroblasts divide asymmetrically multiple times to self-renew and to generate a series of GMCs.
source: Medulla neuroblasts divide asymmetrically multiple times to self-renew and to generate a series of GMCs.
evidence: This is a well-established feature of medulla neuroblast behavior.

claim: The expression pattern of SoxN protein is confined by post-transcriptional mechanisms, as mRNA transcripts are widely distributed but protein is only expressed in the youngest neuroblasts.
source: A case in point is the expression pattern of the SoxN protein recently reported to function alongside Dmrt99B and Hth to specify identities of early-born neurons in the medulla; while mRNA transcripts of the soxN gene are widely distributed in neuroblasts, the SoxN protein is only expressed in the youngest neuroblasts, suggesting that post-transcriptional mechanisms are at work to confine the actual domain of SoxN protein expression (Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The observed patterns of slp1 and slp2 mRNA expression are corroborated by scRNA-seq data.
source: The observed patterns of slp1 and slp2 mRNA expression closely parallel the expression of Slp1 and Slp2 proteins (Figure 1B–D''''), and are also corroborated by scRNA-seq data (Zhu et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The GMR35H02 Gal4 line contains a candidate enhancer driving Slp1/2 expression in medulla neuroblasts.
source: We identified the GMR35H02 Gal4 line as containing a candidate enhancer driving Slp1/2 expression in medulla neuroblasts (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on screening of Gal4 lines and observing GFP expression patterns.

claim: The u8772 220 bp enhancer is contained within the REDfly enhancer u8772.
source: Our analysis of the REDfly enhancers that could potentially regulate expression of Slp1/2 in the medulla also revealed that the 220 bp enhancer segment identified earlier is contained within another REDfly enhancer named u8772 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: Sole deletion of the u8772 220 bp enhancer by CRISPR-Cas9 does not abolish Slp1/2 expression.
source: However, the deletion of this element by CRISPR-Cas9 failed to eliminate the expression of Slp1 and Slp2 in neuroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-A''')
evidence: This is demonstrated by CRISPR deletion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-A'''.

claim: Deletion of the u8772 220 bp enhancer noticeably reduces the expression domain of Slp1.
source: though it noticeably reduced the expression domain of Slp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Sole deletion of the d5778 enhancer by CRISPR-Cas9 does not abolish Slp1/2 expression.
source: As in the case of the u8772 220 bp enhancer deletion, sole deletion of the d5778 enhancer by CRISPR-Cas9 did not abolish Slp1/2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-B''',C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by CRISPR deletion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-B''',C.

claim: The u8772 220 bp and d5778 850 bp enhancers function redundantly and may make additive contributions to attaining the observed levels of Slp1 and Slp2 expression.
source: suggesting that these two enhancers function redundantly and may make additive contributions to attaining the observed levels of Slp1 and Slp2 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of either enhancer alone does not abolish Slp1/2 expression.

claim: The expression of developmentally regulated genes is often controlled by multiple enhancers.
source: Given that the expression of developmentally regulated genes is often controlled by multiple enhancers (Frankel et al., 2010; Fujioka and Jaynes, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Enhancer redundancy is important for achieving robust developmental outcomes.
source: and that enhancer redundancy is important for achieving robust developmental outcomes (Frankel et al., 2010; Ghiasvand et al., 2011; Lagha et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A full complement of stripe enhancers is required for maintaining parasegment boundaries and wingless expression during embryonic segmentation.
source: Although these enhancers share some overlapping functions and domains of activation, a full complement of stripe enhancers is required for maintaining parasegment boundaries and wingless expression (Cadigan et al., 1994; Fujioka and Jaynes, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ey is necessary for activating Slp1/2 expression but not sufficient.
source: It was previously demonstrated that although Ey is necessary for activating Slp1/2 expression it is not sufficient (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: There is always a time delay after the start of Ey expression to the start of Slp expression to ensure the sufficient duration of the Ey window.
source: There is always a time delay after the start of Ey expression to the start of Slp expression to ensure the sufficient duration of the Ey window.
evidence: This is an observation from the expression patterns.

claim: Ey may act by priming the Notch-responsive enhancer of slp providing crucial contextual information, and this is required for Notch to further activate Slp1/2 transcription.
source: Applying these insights to our system, we suggest that Ey may act by priming the Notch-responsive enhancer of slp providing crucial contextual information, and this is required for Notch to further activate Slp1/2 transcription, and speed up the transition (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and insights from other systems.

claim: In Ey stage neuroblasts, Ey is required to initiate Slp expression but not sufficient to activate it to a strong level right away, and after each asymmetric division, activation of Notch signaling in the neuroblast enhances Slp expression, until Slp expression reaches a certain level to repress Ey expression and make the transition.
source: Thus at the Ey to Slp transition, the cell cycle effect is mediated through the direct regulation of Slp transcription by Notch signaling. Taken together, our results suggest that in Ey stage neuroblasts, Ey is required to initiate Slp expression but not sufficient to activate it to a strong level right away, and after each asymmetric division, activation of Notch signaling in the neuroblast enhances Slp expression, until Slp expression reaches a certain level to repress Ey expression and make the transition (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: The mechanism described can be part of a mechanism to coordinate the TTF temporal transition with the cell cycle progression to generate the appropriate number of neural progenies at a given temporal stage.
source: This can be part of a mechanism to coordinate the TTF temporal transition with the cell cycle progression to generate the appropriate number of neural progenies at a given temporal stage.
evidence: This is a proposed function of the mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: In the medulla, blocking cell cycle progression in neuroepithelial cells prematurely transforms them into neuroblasts.
source: Blocking cell cycle progression caused premature transformation of neuroepithelial cells to neuroblasts, as has been previously reported (Zhou and Luo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and observed in the current study.

claim: Cell-cycle arrested neuroblasts produce few progenies.
source: These neuroblasts express the normal neuroblast marker Deadpan (Dpn) (Figure 11A–A'''), but produce few progenies
evidence: This is observed in the PCNA-RNAi experiments shown in Figure 11.

claim: In Su(H) mutant clones, the clone size and neuroblast proliferation are not significantly affected.
source: In the medulla neuroblasts, we also observed that in Su(H) mutant clones, the clone size and neuroblast proliferation are not significantly affected.
evidence: This is observed in the Su(H) mutant clone experiments.

claim: The Notch target gene is lost when cell cycle progression is blocked.
source: On the other hand, we observed that N signaling is dependent on cell-cycle progression, and the Notch target gene is lost when cell cycle progression is blocked.
evidence: This is observed in the PCNA-RNAi experiments.

claim: Notch signaling may affect multiple temporal transitions.
source: Thus N signaling may affect multiple temporal transitions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that expression of earlier and later TTFs is affected by loss of N signaling.

claim: SoxN expression is not significantly affected in Su(H)-RNAi clones.
source: One of the first TTFs, SoxN, is not significantly affected in Su(H)-RNAi clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-A''').
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining SoxN expression in Su(H)-RNAi clones shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-A'''.

claim: In Su(H)-RNAi clones, the first Opa stripe appears expanded, while the second stripe is delayed.
source: Opa, the TTF upstream of Ey, is normally expressed in two stripes. In Su(H)-RNAi clones, the first Opa stripe appears expanded, while the second stripe is delayed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-B''').
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining Opa expression in Su(H)-RNAi clones shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-B'''.

claim: The expression of later factors D and BarH1 are severely delayed or mostly lost when Su(H) is knocked down.
source: Furthermore, the expression of later factors D and BarH1 are severely delayed or mostly lost when we knocked down Su(H) (Figure 5G–H').
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining D and BarH1 expression in Su(H)-RNAi clones shown in Figure 5G-H'.

claim: Genes related to the Notch pathway and participating in the cell division cycle are enriched within the list of genes bound reproducibly both by Ey and by Su(H).
source: Using DAVID, we conducted a functional annotation clustering analysis of this gene list. Genes related to the Notch pathway and participating in the cell division cycle were strikingly enriched within this list of co-bound genes (Supplementary file 6)
evidence: This is based on functional annotation clustering analysis of DamID-seq data.

claim: Ey can function as both transcriptional activator and repressor.
source: thus raising the possibility that in medulla neuroblasts, TTFs such as Ey can modulate the responsiveness of Notch target genes in the medulla to mitogenic Notch signaling as has been seen in Type II neuroblasts (Farnsworth et al., 2015) (note that Ey can function as both transcriptional activator and repressor).
evidence: This is a known property of Ey, supported by a citation.

claim: Only Ey I.D.R peaks were observed in the genomic region of the hmx gene.
source: For example, only Ey I.D.R peaks were observed in the genomic region of the hmx gene (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B), encoding a transcription factor expressed in a type of Notch-off neurons born from the Ey stage (Konstantinides et al., 2022; Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DamID-sequencing experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An I.D.R peak only for Su(H) was found in the dll genomic region.
source: For example, an I.D.R peak only for Su(H) was found in the dll genomic region (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DamID-sequencing experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Notch-on neurons born from the Tll stage neuroblasts express Dll.
source: Since Notch-on neurons born from the Tll stage neuroblasts express Dll (Konstantinides et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Notch pathway may interact with other signaling pathways such as MAPK and BMP in medulla neuroblasts.
source: These preliminary data indicate that the Notch pathway may interact with other signaling pathways such as MAPK and BMP in medulla neuroblasts and present a promising opportunity for future studies.
evidence: This is inferred from the DAVID analysis of genes bound by Su(H).
